clue.text: Sweet drink chasing first of bitters, say

indicators.note: chasing means the drink comes after, following behind the other pieces
first of picks out only the opening letter of the word bitters

parts.note: its first letter is B
to utter something is to say it
Scotch is whisky, a drink

explanation.surface: A bar order: some drink taken after a dash of bitters, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like it describes the drink, but it is the definition, a noun; 'chasing' puts the drink last, as a chaser follows a first drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterscotch is a hard brittle confection of butter and brown sugar, a kind of sweet or candy.

clue.text: Plain landslide, perhaps, for PM

parts.note: bald means plain and unadorned, as in a bald statement
a landslide is an overwhelming victory, an example of a win

explanation.surface: An election result described as a clear landslide for the Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley Baldwin was British Prime Minister three times between the wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Baldwin was a Conservative British Prime Minister in the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Suddenly see shoot

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British informal for suddenly understanding
second meaning: a small shoot from a branch

explanation.surface: Spot something abruptly and fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the verb means to grasp or catch on; as a noun it is a slender growth on a tree.

clue.text: Rank: one he and discontented colonel reviewed

indicators.note: reviewed suggests these letters are looked over again and put into a new order
discontented means the contents are taken out, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: with its insides removed it leaves CL

explanation.surface: Ranks are inspected as a soldier and an unhappy colonel are reviewed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' means unhappy on the surface but here empties colonel to CL; ONE, HE and CL are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a level or grade in an organisation, a tier in a hierarchy.

clue.text: Session: pain hosting it

indicators.note: hosting means holding another inside, as a host holds guests

parts.note: a sting is a sharp pain

explanation.surface: A meeting that is a pain to attend.
explanation.definitionFit: A sitting is a single session of a court, parliament or for a portrait, a period of meeting.

clue.text: Ordinary thing to come from a pen.?

definitions.text: Ordinary thing to come from a pen.?

parts.words: thing to come from a pen
parts.note: ink is what flows out of a writing pen

explanation.surface: A routine product of writing with a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: ink comes from a writing pen, and the grunt comes from a pig pen, an everyday sound for a pig.
explanation.definitionFit: Oink is the grunting noise a pig makes, the usual sound heard from a pigsty.

clue.text: High-jumper in sport?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an insect that leaps

explanation.surface: An athlete who does the high jump in some sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-jumper' suggests an athlete but is the leaping insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricket is a leaping insect related to grasshoppers, and cricket is also the English bat-and-ball game.

clue.text: Proper curry, aloo cooked — yellow perhaps?

parts.note: prim means proper, formally correct

indicators.note: cooked means these letters are mixed up as if prepared in a pan

explanation.surface: A traditional potato curry is cooked, coloured yellow perhaps with turmeric.
explanation.walkthrough: Aloo is the Indian word for potato, so the surface reads as a recipe; 'cooked' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is one of the three basic paint hues from which other colours are mixed, an example of the category.

clue.text: Running repairs put in and returned

indicators.note: repairs means fixing, so the letters are reworked into a new form

explanation.surface: Mechanical fixes were made and the car brought back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running repairs' looks like one phrase, but 'Running' is the definition and 'repairs' the anagram signal for PUT IN plus RETURNED.
explanation.definitionFit: Running means continuous, as in three days running, so it means without a break.

clue.text: Terribly regal, I gathered, monarch's ultimate Elizabethan gentleman

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done badly, so the letters of regal and I are muddled
ultimate means only the last letter of the word is used

parts.note: its last letter is H

explanation.surface: Someone shocked by royal behaviour reports what they heard about an Elizabethan courtier.
explanation.walkthrough: REGAL and I are rearranged to RALEIG, then the last letter of monarch's, H, finishes the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Raleigh was a courtier, explorer and favourite of Queen Elizabeth I.

clue.text: Strain is breaking musical group that's laid back

indicators.note: laid back means lying the other way, so the combined letters are read from right to left
breaking means the word is splits the other word open and sits inside it

parts.note: a nonet is a group of nine musicians

explanation.surface: Stress interrupts a band whose style is very relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid back' pretends to mean relaxed, the opposite of strain, but it turns the whole built word round; a nonet is a nine-piece group.
explanation.definitionFit: Tension is mental or physical strain, the state of being stretched or stressed.

clue.text: Cut beef, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the word we want is pronounced like another one

parts.note: to beef is to complain, to moan

explanation.surface: A butcher's question about a carved piece of beef.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' looks like meat but is the verb to complain; in British speech MOAN and the answer sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Mown is the past participle of mow, so grass that has been mown has been cut.

clue.text: Reportedly flash gift

indicators.note: reportedly means as reported in speech, so the word is one that is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a flare is a sudden flash of light

explanation.surface: Word has it that a flashy present was given.
explanation.definitionFit: A flair for something is a natural talent, an aptitude one has been given.

clue.text: Outer layer broke, almost entirely

indicators.note: almost entirely means the word is used except for its final letter

parts.note: skint is British slang for broke, having no money

explanation.surface: A surface coating has cracked nearly all over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' reads as a verb about breaking but means penniless: SKINT, British slang, loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin is the outer covering of a body or fruit, its outermost layer.

clue.text: Subject on the menu, briefly?

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: what is on the menu is there to pick, to choose from

explanation.surface: A theme that is featured on a restaurant's bill of fare.
explanation.walkthrough: Dishes on a menu are there TO PICK; shortened, that phrase makes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the matter or theme being discussed, the subject of a talk or essay.

clue.text: Tolerate channel

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put up with
second meaning: a small stream, a watercourse

explanation.surface: Put up with a TV station.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to endure or allow, usually negatively; the noun is a small stream flowing in a natural course.

clue.text: Tired and exhausted, descend quickly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ..., worn out and in poor health
second meaning: to ... a slope or stairs

explanation.surface: A weary walker hurries down the hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyphenated, it is an adjective for being worn out; as two words it is the phrasal verb for racing downhill.

clue.text: In attendance, corrupt potential killer

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: in British sport the gate is the attendance at a match
to rot is to decay or corrupt

explanation.surface: Someone present at a scene is crooked and could be a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In attendance' reads as one phrase meaning present, but 'In' is the insertion signal; in British sport the gate is the number of spectators at a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A garotte is a wire or cord used to strangle a person, so it is a weapon capable of killing.

clue.text: Wonderful man sitting at God's right hand

indicators.note: sitting at means placed next to, side by side
on the right hand means this piece comes after, to the right

parts.note: Cor! is a British exclamation, a minced form of God
a king is a man, a piece in chess

explanation.surface: A religious image of a figure seated to the right of the deity.
explanation.walkthrough: The biblical picture of Christ at God's right hand hides a charade: COR, a British exclamation, with KING, a chess man, written to its right.
explanation.definitionFit: Corking is old British slang for excellent or splendid, much like terrific.

clue.text: American mountain, one covered by black cloud?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Mount ..., a volcano in Washington state
second meaning: a place under a black cloud is wetter, more prone to rain

explanation.surface: A US peak, a tall one, shrouded in dark weather.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is whimsical, hence the question mark: something under a dark cloud is likely to be wetter.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Rainier is a volcanic peak near Seattle; as a comparative adjective the word means wetter, more showery.

clue.text: Tramp feeding gobbet to upset crone

indicators.note: feeding means one piece is put into the other, as food goes into a mouth
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: a hag is an ugly old woman, a crone
a gobbet is a lump or chunk

explanation.surface: A vagrant gives a morsel to an old woman who is distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a vagrant but is the verb, to walk heavily; LUMP goes into GAH, which is HAG upset.
explanation.definitionFit: To galumph is to move in a clumsy, heavy-footed way, to stomp or trudge noisily.

clue.text: Iris or Lily for example dropped brick?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: something that blooms, a flower
second meaning: a gaffe, as in dropping a brick, a blunder

explanation.surface: Two women's names and an accident on a building site.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris and Lily look like women's names but are flowers; to drop a brick is British for making a tactless blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a plant that flowers, and also informal British for an embarrassing mistake.

clue.text: Far Eastern symbol of loyalty, promise of marriage to US president?

indicators.note: to means joined on next, as this piece is attached after

parts.note: Bush was the name of two US presidents
I do is the vow said at a wedding

explanation.surface: A US president proposes, a Far Eastern gesture of loyalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Bushido is the Japanese samurai code of honour, which put loyalty to one's master above all.

clue.text: Very tasty, as Othello in speech?

indicators.note: in speech means as spoken, so the word sounds like another

parts.note: Othello was a Moor, so he is Moorish

explanation.surface: A query whether Othello's lines are delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello, Shakespeare's Moor, is MOORISH, which in British speech sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Moreish is British informal for food so delicious that you want more of it.

clue.text: Some territorials, travelling westward, retreat

indicators.note: in an across clue westward is right to left, so the letters run backwards
some means only a part of the word is taken, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: Part-time soldiers heading west fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' seems to continue the military story but is the noun, a hideaway. Territorials are the British part-time Territorial Army.
explanation.definitionFit: A lair is a den where a wild animal retreats to rest or hide, a place of refuge.

clue.text: Load of fun, dammit!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a thoroughly enjoyable time
second meaning: ...! is a mild curse of annoyance

explanation.surface: An exclamation of irritation after a good time.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is informal for a great time; as an interjection it is a mild oath like curses.

clue.text: Activate mind-blowing experience

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to ... a switch or alarm is to set it off
second meaning: a drug-induced hallucinatory experience

explanation.surface: Switch on something that will blow your mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense is setting off a mechanism; the noun sense is slang for a psychedelic episode on drugs.

clue.text: Astronomical body in second lit up

parts.note: a mo is British informal for a moment, a second
a light that is lit up is on

explanation.surface: A heavenly body shining a moment later.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, and a moon is any planet's satellite, a celestial body.

clue.text: Queen Cleopatra, nightly, bathes

indicators.note: bathes means the words wrap around the answer like bath water, holding it within

explanation.surface: Cleopatra takes a bath every night.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleopatra famously bathed in asses' milk, which is the picture here.
explanation.definitionFit: A rani is an Indian queen or the wife of a rajah.

clue.text: Identical class of undergraduates?

parts.note: undergraduates attend uni, the university
in British schools a form is a class

explanation.surface: A query whether a group of students all look the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' is also clothing, which is what the surface hints at; here it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniform as an adjective means the same throughout, unvarying, alike in every case.

clue.text: Picture — take it

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to picture something is to form a mental image of it
second meaning: I take it means I suppose, I assume

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit the verb: visualising something in the mind, and supposing or presuming, as in I take it so.

clue.text: "Chic" dresses half limp — this adds shine

indicators.note: dresses means one piece clothes the other, wrapping it around

parts.note: in quotes, chic is a word that is French, and as a word it means posh

indicators.note: half means only the first half of the word is used

parts.note: its first half is LI

explanation.surface: A stylish outfit is made to cover a weak, floppy part to give it gloss.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotes matter: "Chic" is itself a French word, giving FRENCH, and chic means POSH; LI, half of limp, goes inside POSH.
explanation.definitionFit: French polish is a shellac finish applied to wooden furniture to give it a high gloss.
